results.note: All parts match p. 117 (rendered). Marshall's statements verified (p. 1434 supply, p. 1435 policing); ref. 44 (p. 1437) matches letter ref. 3 but for the year. The letter's '12 months' misstates Kerr's 6-month question (Kerr, p. 40).

results.corrected_extracted: The authors note a decline over time in the proportion of participants reporting a non-fatal overdose, the most substantial during 2001, and write that it is consistent with other reports of a reduction in heroin-related overdoses during this period (Wood et al., 2006, as cited) and suggests that global reductions in heroin supply may have played a role; it may also be related to the protective effect of methadone treatment and the significant expansion of methadone treatment availability in British Columbia from 1995 to 2004 (Anderson and Warren, 2004, as cited). They also note that a supervised injection facility had recently opened in Vancouver and that its impact on overdose had not yet been evaluated. Limitations: VIDUS is not a random sample, so the findings may not generalize to other populations of people who inject drugs; overdoses were self-defined by participants asked whether they had had an overdose in the past 6 months, an approach the authors say may introduce an element of subjectivity but offers advantages where polysubstance use is the norm, adding that the definitions used in previous studies also introduce limitations related to recall bias and do not provide a hard diagnosis of overdose; the exact temporal relationship between the outcome and the explanatory variables could not be ascertained, so the study does not allow a thorough investigation of causal relationships; and although it has been suggested that changing drug purity may play a role in predicting overdose (Darke et al., 1999, as cited), the authors were unable to consider it. Editors' notes: the study recorded no measure of heroin supply, availability, price or purity, so its explanation of the decline rests on the papers it cites. The letter (anchor 9) says these authors clearly point to reduced heroin supply as the reason; the paper says reduced supply may have played a role and adds methadone expansion as a possible reason. The paper it cites for the reduction in heroin-related overdoses (Wood et al., 2006, volume 101, pages 689–95, on Canadian heroin supply) is the letter's reference 3, dated 2004 there, and the study's own reference 44 (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 1434, 1437); read since from its PDF (anchors 19 to 22), it reports fewer overdose deaths across British Columbia in 2001–03 than in 1998–2000 and fewer naloxone-requiring ambulance responses in the Downtown Eastside in fiscal 2001–02 to 2002–03 than in fiscal 1997–98 to 2000–01, and measured no heroin purity.
results.note: Only the closing comparison is fixed: Wood's naloxone series compares fiscal 2001–02 to 2002–03 with fiscal 1997–98 to 2000–01, not 2001–03 with 1998–2000 (Wood, pp. 690–691). All other parts confirmed on pp. 41–44 (rendered).

results.corrected_extracted: A paper by five authors, three of them authors of the study (Wood, Montaner and Kerr), on markers of heroin use and harm in western Canada before and after the Australian heroin shortage, which it dates from about January 2001. Its stated primary hypothesis was that the markers would stay stable or rise, because western Canada receives heroin from similar source countries and, citing one paper, had not measurably changed its supply-reduction funding or activities since the mid-1990s. It compared yearly averages, with no statistical test and no comparison series, of overdose deaths in the whole province of British Columbia from the provincial vital statistics registry, 1998–2000 against 2001–03 (the drugs responsible were not available, and some deaths would probably not involve heroin); ambulance responses that required naloxone in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside, fiscal years 1997–98 to 2000–01 against 2001–02 to 2002–03; and the weight of heroin destined for Canada that was seized, 1998–2000 against 2001–03, a potential indicator of supply that, the authors note, could also mark supply-reduction activity. In VIDUS, a prospective cohort of people who inject drugs in Vancouver interviewed every 6 months, daily heroin use reported from May 1996 to December 2004 was compared between 1996–2000 and 2001–04 by GEE logistic regression, with potential confounders including methadone use and residence in the Downtown Eastside. Editors' note: the death series is titled drug-induced deaths in its source (reference 19, p. 694); no series measures heroin purity, price or availability directly, none covers an area smaller than the Downtown Eastside, and none goes beyond 2003 (December 2004 for the cohort); the paper's text does not discuss supervised injection, which appears only in the title of its reference 24 (p. 695), a 2005 paper on safer injection facility use cited with reference 23 for the cohort's description (p. 691).
results.note: Two fixes: the Methods say funding and activities had not changed measurably (p. 690); and reference 24's title (p. 695), cited for the cohort, names safer injection facility use. All else confirmed on rendered pages.

results.corrected_extracted: The authors conclude that massive decreases in markers of heroin use were seen in western Canada coinciding with the Australian heroin shortage, despite no increases in funding to Canadian enforcement efforts, and that these findings suggest external global heroin supply forces deserve greater investigation and credence as a potential explanation of the Australian shortage; they acknowledge that supply may instead have been diverted elsewhere, or production switched to other drugs such as methamphetamine. Limitations they state: overdose statistics and seizure data may be poor proxies for heroin use; the measures were not counted at the same level, and fiscal years put 4 months of post-shortage data in the period before the shortage for naloxone; Canada has no standardized longitudinal measures of street heroin purity, although other studies (cited) found ambulance visits and overdose mortality statistics to correlate strongly with street purity. Funding: the cohort is supported by the US National Institutes of Health and the Canadian Institutes of Health Research; the article has no conflict-of-interest statement. Editors' note: the paper's evidence for unchanged Canadian enforcement is one citation, with no data shown; its statement that reduced heroin availability on Vancouver's streets was widely reported in the media cites a paper on HIV treatment (its reference 17); it measured neither heroin purity nor price.

key_findings.correction: Data sources: overdose deaths (the paper's term; its source, ref. 19, is titled drug-induced deaths) for the whole of British Columbia, 1998–2003, from the provincial vital statistics agency (the drugs responsible were not available, and the authors expect some deaths not to involve heroin); ambulance responses requiring naloxone in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside, by fiscal year, 1997–98 to 2002–03; heroin destined for Canada that was seized, 1998–2003, as a potential indicator of supply that could also mark supply-reduction activity. Periods compared: 1998–2000 against 2001–03; for naloxone, four fiscal years (1997–98 to 2000–01) against two (2001–02 to 2002–03).

Yearly averages (Table 1): overdose deaths in British Columbia 297 in 1998–2000 against 192 in 2001–03 (35.4% reduction); naloxone-requiring ambulance responses in the Downtown Eastside 674 a year in fiscal 1997–98 to 2000–01 against 370 in 2001–02 to 2002–03 (45.1%); heroin destined for Canada seized 184 kg a year against 67 kg (63.6%). No intervals or statistical tests.

finding: Figure 1 prints no values. Editors' reading at 300 dpi (approximate): overdose deaths in British Columbia about 399 (1998), 272 (1999), 218 (2000), 221 (2001), 169 (2002) and 186 (2003); naloxone-requiring responses in the Downtown Eastside about 732 (fiscal 1997–98), 840 (1998–99), 655 (1999–2000), 464 (2000–01), 388 (2001–02) and 350 (2002–03); heroin seized about 234, 142, 177, 94, 46 and 60 kg (1998 to 2003). Means by period from these readings: 296 and 192 deaths, 673 and 369 responses, 184 and 67 kg, each within 1 of Table 1. | note: Bar tops read inside the 0.96-point bar outlines (the outer edge of a bar reads about 2 deaths, 4 responses or 1 kg higher) against the fitted axis ticks; cross-checked against the bar rectangles drawn in the PDF, which agree within 1 for deaths and seizures and within 2 for naloxone responses (rectangles about 733–734, 841, 655, 465, 388 and 350–351). Approximate to about ±1 death, ±2 responses and ±0.5 kg.

Coverage: the routine series end in 2003 (fiscal 2002–03 for naloxone) and the cohort in December 2004; no figure is given for 2005, for Vancouver's overdose deaths or for any area smaller than the Downtown Eastside, and the text does not discuss supervised injection: it appears only in the title of reference 24 (p. 695), a 2005 paper on safer injection facility use cited with reference 23 for the cohort's description (p. 691).

Authors' conclusions: deaths and naloxone use fell markedly in western Canada at about the time of the Australian shortage, corroborated by the cohort's fall in heroin use; seizures fell by more than 60%; that Canada saw a similar reduction without increasing supply-reduction efforts, they write, suggests that external global heroin supply forces deserve much greater investigation and credence as a potential explanation of the Australian shortage. They acknowledge that supply may instead have been diverted elsewhere or production switched to other drugs such as methamphetamine.

reporting_issues.correction: issue: The cohort's breakdown of 1997–2004 by quarter is four two-year periods, given as shares without counts or a stated denominator (people or interviews); the outcome is named inconsistently: daily heroin use in the abstract's Methods, the Methods and the Results sentences on data points and shares, and daily injection of heroin, injection of heroin or daily heroin injection in the abstract's Results, the Results sentence on the odds ratio and Table 2 (pp. 689, 691, 693). | consequence: The yearly course of daily heroin injection, including 2001 on its own, cannot be recovered from the paper.

risk_of_bias.note: Agree with prospective-cohort and ROBINS-E (the card says three of the four series are aggregate counts) and with overall high. Minor: the confounding note says the cohort model has no term for ageing, but age is adjusted for (Table 2 footnote, p. 693); time in the cohort and turnover are not.

interpretation_gap.note: Agree: substantial. Gap (5) says slightly more than the paper: the authors acknowledge only the lack of standardized purity measures (p. 694), not of price or availability data.

missed: Label: the card calls the death series drug-induced deaths throughout (design_detail, can_establish, recruitment, outcomes, effect_sizes, interpretation gap, where_it_stands; KF1, KF3, KF4). The paper's own term is overdose deaths or overdose mortality (pp. 689–692; Table 1 row 'Annual mortality'; Figure 1A); drug-induced deaths is the title of its source (ref. 19, p. 694). Keep the paper's term and give the source title once.

Supervised injection: design_detail and cannot_establish say the paper does not mention it, but reference 24 (p. 695; Kerr et al., 2005, Lancet 366, 316–318) is titled on safer injection facility use; it is cited, with reference 23, only for the cohort's description (p. 691).

where_it_stands calls this the only source on file for yearly deaths in British Columbia around 2001. The letter on file (Christian et al., 2012, p. 117, Figure; its ref. 2, a provincial report on illicit drug deaths) plots yearly overdose deaths for all of British Columbia, 1997–2007. Editors' reading of its vector line: about 416 (1998), 277 (1999), 247 (2000), 245 (2001), 170 (2002) and 190 (2003), against this paper's about 400, 272, 218, 221, 169 and 186. In both series 2001 is level with 2000.

Unlisted inconsistencies: the abstract counts three independent markers of heroin use (p. 689), the Discussion four independent markers of heroin market activity (p. 692); the abstract's Methods presents seizures as an overall marker of Canadian supply reduction (p. 689), while the Results and Discussion read their fall as reduced supply (pp. 691–694); Figure 1C's caption says heroin seized in Canada (p. 692), where the Methods and Table 1 say heroin destined for Canada (pp. 690–691).

Timeline, 2012 reply: the reply says its stable-use data were referenced in the original report (Marshall et al., 2012, p. 118), but the original report's reference 44 is this paper (101: 689–95), not the 623–625 paper the reply cites; worth stating in that entry.

extra.note: Reference 44 is cited twice, both on p. 1434, in the paragraph that also says the authors have no evidence of significant changes in drug supply or purity (that sentence has no citation); p. 1435 repeats, without a citation, that community drug-use patterns and other interventions showed no apparent change. Wood et al. (2006) contains none of the four: its cohort data end in December 2004, with nothing for 2005; it reports daily heroin use falling, not constant (adjusted odds ratio 0.55 for 2001–04 against 1996–2000; 36.5%, 32.6%, 23.3% and 20.8% for 1997/98 to 2003/04; p. 691 and Table 2, p. 693) and methamphetamine use rising (data not shown, p. 691); it gives no yearly figures for daily cocaine injection, methadone or other treatment, using daily cocaine injection and current methadone use only as covariates (Table 2, p. 693). Its nearest figures are 23.3% (2001/02) and 20.8% (2003/04) reporting daily use. The authors' reply (Marshall et al., 2012, p. 118; references on p. 119) cites for stable daily heroin use from 2001 to 2005 a different paper by the same five authors (Addiction 2006; 101: 623–25) and a 2009 web report, and says these data were referenced in the original report; neither is in the PDF folder. The letter (Christian et al., 2012, p. 117, its reference 3) cites the same 689–95 paper, dated 2004, for higher heroin availability until 2001.
